profiles.meeting_scenario: An internal troubleshooting meeting at a university-industry ML lab two weeks before a camera-ready deadline for the ZNorm paper extension. The team has integrated ZNorm into the lab's current PyTorch training stack to reproduce the reported CIFAR-10 ResNet results, but the new runs show erratic early-epoch behavior, little apparent acceleration, and inconsistent gains across seeds. The agenda is to diagnose why the current implementation does not look like the original results, determine whether the issue is in the implementation, the evaluation protocol, or the comparison setup, and agree on a concrete debugging plan. The expected outcome is a short list of checks and reruns that both participants believe will resolve the discrepancy and confirm that ZNorm is 'working.'

members.name: Dr. Lina Park
members.role: Postdoctoral Researcher and lead author on ZNorm
members.expertise: Optimization methods for deep networks, gradient dynamics, experimental design for training-method papers
members.background: Lina developed the original ZNorm prototype in a smaller research codebase and ran most of the paper experiments on CIFAR-10 and a medical imaging segmentation setup; she now needs a clean reproduction in the lab's unified training framework for the extended submission.
members.private_state: She wants the new reproduction to preserve the paper's core claim that ZNorm reaches target accuracy in fewer updates without changing architecture, and she is worried that infrastructure differences are obscuring that effect rather than revealing a real flaw in the method.
hidden_assumptions: When people say ZNorm 'accelerates training,' they mean it reaches a target validation accuracy in fewer optimizer updates, even if per-step wall-clock time is slightly worse.
A 'baseline' comparison should refer to the original plain-SGD-like training setup from the paper era, not the lab's newer optimized stack with mixed precision and fused data pipelines.

If someone says the method is inserted 'before the optimizer step,' that implies operating on the fully accumulated, unscaled gradient tensor for the effective batch, not on each microbatch contribution.
A result 'matches the paper' if the best-checkpoint performance and convergence pattern are consistent across a small multi-seed average, rather than a single run's final epoch.

members.name: Ravi Menon
members.expertise: PyTorch distributed training, AMP, optimizer hooks, experiment pipelines, reproducibility tooling
members.background: Ravi maintains the lab's standardized training repo and integrated ZNorm into the existing optimizer/gradient-processing path so it can run on the same infrastructure as other methods with DDP, AMP, gradient accumulation, and standardized reporting.
members.private_state: He wants to avoid special-case code paths and prove the method works in the modern production-like stack; he is concerned that if ZNorm only looks good under a legacy setup or custom measurement protocol, it will be fragile and hard to maintain.
hidden_assumptions: When researchers say a method 'accelerates training,' they normally mean reduced wall-clock time to a target metric under the current standard stack, since that is what users experience.
The relevant 'baseline' is the lab's current canonical ResNet training recipe, because that is the fairest apples-to-apples comparison in the repo.
If a method is applied 'before the optimizer step,' using the existing gradient hook on each accumulated backward pass is equivalent enough unless someone explicitly says otherwise.
A run 'reproduces' once the standard reporting pipeline shows a comparable final test accuracy on a representative single seed, because that is how infra validation is usually done.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both discuss whether ZNorm is 'accelerating training' or improving 'time to target.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means fewer optimizer updates or epochs to reach a target validation accuracy, regardless of a small per-step compute overhead.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means lower wall-clock time to reach the target under the standard training stack, including AMP and systems overhead.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In ML meetings, 'faster training' and 'time to target' are often used loosely and treated as interchangeable, so each hears a familiar phrase and assumes the other shares the same operational meaning.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer to 'the baseline' and 'the plain ResNet run.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the original paper-era baseline in the legacy repo: FP32, no fused augmentations, no EMA, and the exact old scheduler defaults.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the current canonical repo baseline: AMP on, gradient accumulation logic enabled by default, fused preprocessing, and the latest scheduler wrapper.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both baselines are reasonable and familiar within the lab, and 'the baseline' sounds singular and settled, so neither expects the reference to be ambiguous.

misalignment_points.topic: Where ZNorm is applied in the gradient path
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to 'apply ZNorm before the optimizer step' and talk about the existing gradient hook.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes ZNorm is computed once on the final accumulated gradient after AMP unscaling and after all microbatches for the effective batch have contributed.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes using the repo's gradient-processing hook on each backward pass during accumulation is still 'before the optimizer step' and therefore compatible.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both descriptions are technically true at a high level, and the phrase 'before the optimizer step' is common shorthand that hides important ordering details inside modern training stacks.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to match the paper
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both talk about whether the new runs 'match the paper' or whether the reproduction is 'good enough.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the best-checkpoint result and early convergence shape should align with the reported trend over multiple seeds within expected variance.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a single standard pipeline run should end near the reported final accuracy, even if the curve shape and best-vs-last checkpoint behavior differ.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both standards sound like ordinary reproducibility criteria, and because they are troubleshooting rather than writing the evaluation section, neither feels a need to formalize the acceptance rule.

If that signal disappears in the unified framework, I need to know whether the stack changed the gradient path or whether we're comparing against the wrong training setup.
